review:
This is my first steam review, and it probably won't be read in the sea of other comments on this title, but I felt that despite years of gaming (okay, decades) I've never felt the urge to strongly recommend a purchase until now. Sure, there are things I would have preferred to be more complex, spoilt by the combat systems of Dark souls and the Witcher, but what's so special about this game is the storytelling and the creative courage Ninja Theory bring. 

This isn't just a game. This is a sincere artwork, using game design, to tell the most compelling story about psychosis I've ever experienced. They did their homework, not just with the depiction of mental illness, but also on the wonderful Norse mythology, joyously wrestled from the bubblegum claws of Marvel studios and told with all its blood and guts and grim darkness. 

Senua is easily the most human heroine I've seen in any game ever, and while there have been more 'strong' female characters, there's no heroism like the heroism of the truly broken and crippled. She has to fight her demons, and it's all the more meaningful because unlike fem-Shepard who eats Reapers for breakfast, you can see in the gorgeously motion captured performance of Senua's face, that she is truly terrified as she fights. 

This game is short. This game probably has awful replay value. All the same, this game is a MUST play.

Just completed the game and played with sound cancelling head phones the entire way. The most intense, surreal, deep and rewarding game I have ever had played in my life. If you haven't got it, get it.﻿

This is the single best game I have ever played in my life and i've been gaming since the 80s. Ninja Theory used Cambridge Professors of mental health and actual people with mental health issues to make this as real as they could. Senua sufers from psychosis. She hears voices, sees patterns and numbers in the world around her. 

  I have never been big on puzzle and story games. What if I didn't ilke the story? I wasted my money. The "puzzles" in this game don't really feel like puzzles... the "story" is amazing... the fighting sequences are awesome! There is a great balance of all of these things in the game. It's not all "puzzles" not all fighting and not all story. Beautifully balanced.

  The voices... oh man.. the voices make the buildup insane! And when they aren't there for brief moments, you actually feel alone. If your thinking "i don't want to buy a game that only has 10 hours of play time" (or whatever) I am with you on that! I never puchase a game that I see low hours on, but this is not a full priced 60 dollar game, but you the get triple A title treatment. 

   This game is absolutely gorgeous. I am still running a 970 for a graphics card and I can play at full settings and its beautiful. I don't know how they pulled it off.. optimization? This just goes to show you how poorly optimized other games are. 

   YOU MUST USE HEADPHONES or a really good surround sound. Very few games have ever made me actually turn my head while playing when I hear something. For the best use simulated our actual surround sound headphones. 

  My final take? Let me tell you about myself so this might actually means something. I am a Marine Corps combat Veteran. I own and operate my own dump trucking business. I am a "hard" man. This game had me balling and blubbering at the end. I was yelling at my screen "I WIL NOT GIVE UP, NO, I WILL NOT GIVE UP!!!!" I have felt "feelings" about this game for days after beating it. I have changed my destop background. I have played through 1.75 times (had to format PC) and I will play through again for sure!

  I highly encourage you to research this game before you play. Understand the background because it will make you FEEL so much more. 

  I simply cannot put into words how this game takes you into the world of psychosis, mental illness, and at the same time give you a great story about a small clan that was conquered by Vikings,, aka "The Northman" and one persons fight against her own demons in her head.

  Hellblade gets 5 thumbs up from me. Best game I have ever played in my life, yes I know, I said that already and I MEAN IT.  Also, I rarely write reviews, like never.

The quick and dirty recommendation guide (pick as many +/- points as you like and make up your mind if it's worth buying):
+ strong narrative
+ outstanding sound and visual presentation
+ responsive, intense and simple combat
+ nightmarish horror atmosphere (without jump scares)
+ superb voice acting
+ frightening and well-designed end bosses
+/- combat lacks complexity and may be too simple for some
+/- no replay value (it may have for a revisited experience)
+/- bit short, which is compensated by fair price and gameplay without tedious and lengthy grinds
+/- high stylized presentation of events and plot may not be everyone's taste (totally mine, though)
- gameplay doesn't offer much variety
- not much to explore apart from lore stones telling you about Norse mythology (which is quite important, however!)
- lack of variety in enemies and their appearance

The details:

Hellblade tells a story about suffering, sacrifice, darkness and endeavor. Following the story of Picts warrior maid Senua, you embark on a nightmarish and mind-twisting journey to Helheim, to save a beloved one’s soul. However, for Senua, many things aren’t what they’re supposed to be, for she’s suffering from severe psychosis. While you often can’t decide what’s real and what not, you must overcome many obstacles and enemies – the latter seemingly coming right out of Hel(l).

No other game, up to this point, managed to devour me – getting me so immersed – like Hellblade did. This game just pulled me deeper than any other game has accomplished in recent years, and I, mentally, switched off everything else around me and Senua’s reality became mine. The sound design and visual presentation is outstanding.

I was always a fan of non-linear storytelling and Hellblade totally nailed it. Its presentation is intriguing, captivating and keep you ever so interested in what happened (to Senua) and how everything will turn out.

As for the gameplay I was kind of surprised of what they came up with: There's a level where there is nothing but darkness and you have to find your way out, without fighting, only using your senses, as Senua's reaching out with her hand to frisk her surroundings, or running from one light source to another to not getting devoured by darkness. In other parts, cynically spoken, you could call it 'walking simulator', but, as for myself, I was so immersed in the world that I didn't mind. It doesn’t deliver any boredom even when ‘nothing’ happens.

There is one thing to explore off the main paths, however: Lore stones. These stones – telling you about Norse mythology in appearance of an old friend – are optional but critical in further expanding on the whole game’s story. At first one might not see the entangled meaning of Norse mythology and it seems rather random, just to give this game a Norse touch although you're not playing a viking heroine. Certainly, Vikings are involved in the story but that doesn’t necessarily explain why you keep hearing stories about the Northmen. But keep your wits about you and you’ll come to realize the importance of those stories.

I also enjoyed the combat, although it lacks complexity and deep mechanics. So, what is to like about it? Its responsiveness and simplicity made it a blast to play. It is quick, brutal, intense and it just works without any clumsiness. In that regard it is sort of 'flawless', straight on point. Don't expect anything near like Dark Souls, though.

Visual clues were used in a clever way and weren't spelled out boldly for you with exclamation marks, compass needles and the like. Even in one given situation where acting under pressure and time limit was required, I managed to find all the necessary clues at the first try without said compass needle or other HUD markers pointing out where to go – there are voices telling you to "focus" or to look in another direction. The lack of (almost) any meta information fits the theme of the game and it is an enjoyable change in a video game. That being said, there's no "meta game" telling you how to do things (apart from the game options menu). No HUD, no text boxes or pop ups. Everything you need to know to beat the game is offered by the environments and from 'within' the game.

It absolutely has become one of my favorite games by now.

[b] Do not play without HEADPHONES. AT. ALL. [/b] EDIT: The real fun for me was actually sometimes ending up looking back hearing a "Watch out" over the headphones. You may have an awesome sound system (I dont) but still, the experience changes a lot over headphones.

[b] FYI - There is a lot of walking and finding symbols, easy puzzle solving with an easy to master combat. If that isnt your type of game,you probably wont like this. If you seek Environment, Immersion, Good story - Welcome home my friend. You & me both found what we were looking for. [/b]

Woah, I don't know what to feel.

The ending was a bit too much for me.  
I was trying to not cry when the credits began rolling, but with the singer saying "please don't cry now" in the very same moment, this attempt wasn't successful in the slightest.

But let's talk about the game itself:
The game tells a very unique story about mental health and psychosis (which you probably already know). It does this amazingly well while blending in the other gameplay elements.
The atmosphere, mainly created by the voice acting, is impeccable. Absolutely outstanding.
The graphics, fights and everything else are pretty good but nothing outstanding (at least currently, the graphics were probably more impressive at launch). The puzzles become repetitive after a while but it's not too bad. 

But what annoyed me the most about this game was a lack of guidance at times.
The game has next to no HUD (which it solves 99% of the time pretty well) but I have spent numerous times looking where to go or what the game wanted me to do, that I had to lookup a walkthough video.

It caused me to anticipate for the game to end while playing, leaving the game to rot in my library for 2 years until finally finishing it now and overall degrading the experience. 
Because of this I cannot piece together the full story afterwards, which is sad.
I feel bad for saying it, but I'm glad that I'm finally done and I can uninstall it.

So, overall, I did not enjoy this game as much as I hoped I would, except the ending, which made me very emotional.

This isn't a video game. It's an interactive panic attack.

Play alone in the dark with headphones, and don't feel ashamed if you have to step away and take a break.

[h1]“The hardest battles are fought in the mind, not with the sword.”[/h1]

Following Senua on a journey into Helheim with hopes of rescuing her dead lover, we are actually following her deep within her own mind and witnessing her descent into madness. With psychosis as Hellblade’s central theme, I was constantly questioning what was real and what wasn’t. What was a Celtic warrior doing in a Norse realm? How much could I trust the voices of the Furies? How much could I trust the game’s threat of permadeath? How much of the game was a delusion or just a manifestation of Senua’s mind? Would I even get answers?

In the end it didn’t matter, because it was all real for Senua. Unreliable narrators, voices that suggest conflicting thoughts to make you doubt yourself, seeing and hearing things that no one else can see, feeling alone… the game puts you in Senua’s frame of mind and makes you feel fear, dread, anxiety. I have never been so deeply affected by a game and a singular character as I have by Hellblade, and Senua. This game explores mental health in an incredibly complex, clever, bold and RESPECTFUL way that was obviously well-researched and that I found to be incredibly enlightening. I would argue this game is a landmark in videogame storytelling. How many stories have you seen/read where Senua would not be the heroine, but a villain? What better medium to get people to truly understand how psychosis might look/feel/sound than a videogame?

The use of tense atmosphere, binaural sound to replicate auditory hallucinations, and Melina Juergens’ amazing performance as Senua put me in the game in such a way that I found it difficult to leave. Senua’s terrifying screams, uncomfortable levels of pure fear, tangible suffering – how can you experience that and then put the game down to go eat a f*cking snack? I mean, I did, it’s like a 7 hour game, but even though I left the game, it didn’t leave me. The stress and terror lingered. I played this game for the first time in 2017 on PS4 and I never stopped thinking about it.
 
I recommend you overlook any negative complaints regarding gameplay elements and just experience Senua’s haunting vision quest for yourself. I feel the story is strong enough and the game short enough that these things shouldn’t be detrimental. That said, I personally enjoyed the gameplay. The puzzles are easy, nothing you’ll get stuck on, but they’re new and different and kinda neat. The combat is easy as well, but punchy and fast and stylish and satisfying. If your reflexes are fast and you can parry every swing that comes down at you, you will be blowing through combat very quickly. While the puzzles and combat occasionally felt a bit obligatory, I enjoyed that I was given a break from the nightmare. Horror films aren’t scary visual after scary visual, or you’d become numb to the scares. You have to give the moments of horror time to breathe for maximum effectiveness. They need time to sink in, time to make you feel calm and secure, before grabbing you by your neck again. 

[h1]"You think you can overcome the darkness. Make sense of it. And once relief settles in, it strikes out of nowhere, throwing you helplessly back into the maelstrom.”[/h1]

Hellblade is a third person action game where the player controls a Celtic woman called Senua, who is fighting through Hell to rescue the soul of her dead lover from the Norse gods.

The melee combat system is really enjoyable. You’re armed with a sword, and you’ve got four basic moves – quick attack, strong attack, dodge and parry. You can also charge up a focus mode, where time slows down but you still attack at normal speed. There are a few different enemies to fight including one armed with a sword, one with a mace, another with a mace and shield, one who dual wields small axes, and a big dude with a massive two handed axe. And of course there are a few unique bosses.

The key to success is to watch your opponent’s movements to anticipate their attacks (there are no flashing icons above their heads here), dodge or parry, and then follow up with your own attacks while their guard is down. The quality of the character animations allows you to really feel the weight behind every hit, especially when Senua gets knocked down, and when she blocks an attack, causing the enemy to stumble backwards.

Hellblade has a kind of permadeath mechanic in place. You’ve got an unspecified amount of lives, and each time you die, a dark black “rot” grows up Senua’s right arm. If it reaches her brain, she dies permanently and your save will be deleted. This adds an intensity to the combat, and makes you want to play cautiously instead of just rushing in and button mashing. However, its not something that you need to be scared of, or a reason to avoid playing the game. I beat Hellblade in one playthrough, and I’d guess I died around ten times. Even the later fights, where you’ll be up against multiple enemies (at one point I was simultaneously fighting eight enemies on a narrow bridge), aren’t too hard if you make intelligent use of focus.

The other primary gameplay mechanic is puzzle solving, but the quality of these is a bit of a mixed bag. The most common type of puzzle requires you to find “runes” to unlock doors. These runes are hidden somewhere in the environment. For example, a letter N might be formed by two tree trunks and a tree branch. You need to stand in the correct spot and then focus your vision on the shape of the rune. Its not a particularly interesting mechanic, and the game solves 90% of the puzzle for you anyway, because you’ll see a bunch of red runes floating in the general area where you need to stand.

The better kind of puzzles involves interacting with objects to change the layout of the environment. For example, your path might be blocked by the illusion of a wall, until you look through an archway which dispels the illusion. In another area, you’ll look through masks to switch back and forth between day and night, to bypass obstacles that are blocking your path.

Throughout the game, you’ll frequently hear several whispered voices, which seem to be a representation of Senua’s internal hopes, doubts and fears. These voices are sometimes helpful or supportive, but mostly they taunt you and try to make you doubt yourself. During combat, when an enemy gets behind you they’ll warn you to “watch out”, but when you take damage they’ll say “she’s going to die”. As you’re wandering around the environment, they’ll claim “she’s going the wrong way, she’s lost”. These voices sound really cool and I can’t remember this being done by any other game that I’ve played.

Senua’s facial expressions might be the best I’ve ever seen in a game. I felt like I could understand her emotional state, especially pain, fear and sadness, just by looking at her face. The way her eyes move makes her seem alive, especially when she looks directly at the camera, and lip syncing is a perfect match to the dialogue. If every game was like this, we could forget about the uncanny valley. Senua’s voice actress, Melina Juergens, also gives a phenomenal performance.

The environments are absolutely gorgeous. Generally I don’t really care about graphical quality, I’m more focused on gameplay and story. But there were times when even I had to stop for a moment and say “wow”. Occasionally you’ll be outside in bright sunlight, looking at a colourful field of flowers. But mostly you’ll be surrounded by ruined buildings full of burnt corpses, or in dark caves, the floor covered in bones, with only a small torch to light the way ahead.

However, I think the area layouts could be better. Many modern games design levels in a kind of circle. When you reach the end of a section, they’ll find an elegant way to quickly get you back to the start, for example through a previously locked door, or by dropping down from a higher platform. In Hellblade, particularly after defeating a boss, you just have to spend about 5 minutes backtracking through the areas you’ve just cleared, with absolutely nothing happening. There’s not much space to explore, and the only reason to do this anyway is to find stone markers that tell you small pieces of stories which are not at all related to Senua, and mostly fall into the category of “a long time ago, this guy you’ve never met and don’t care about did a thing to this other guy you’ve never met and don’t care about”.

I easily maintained a constant 60 fps with all settings maxed at 1080p, and I didn’t suffer from any bugs or crashes. However, you can’t fully rebind controls on a keyboard. In particular, you can’t rebind movement to arrow keys, which is my preferred setup. Instead, I played with my 360 gamepad which worked great.

Overall, while I’m not quite as in love with this game as most of the critics, I did find alot to enjoy, so I’d recommend Hellblade to any fan of action games. As it only took me 8.5 hours to complete the game, I’d suggest waiting for a sale of around 25-33%.

The author's thoughts on life, religion and death are reflected in senua's growth, which is also conveyed to the players through this novel and resonates with them. Meanwhile, the ending is thought-provoking.
But if you think of the game as an action game, or if you don't have the psychological ability, this game may not be for you. Five minutes of fighting, two hours of deciphering. At the same time, the whole process of the game feel heavy depression, may cause discomfort in a part of the crowd.

Hellblade might be the most atmospheric game I’ve played in years. Ninja Theory combines Norse mythology with the beautifully developed character Senua, who is plagued by psychosis. She hears whispering voices. Lots of them. All the time. Those voices tell her what to do, or what not to do. Sometimes they reveal things from Senua’s past, tell little stories, other times they try to encourage her, or even predict her certain demise. Only one thing is certain – they won’t stop talking. Not ever. They are also the main reason why you absolutely should play the game with a headset.

This is in my eyes Hellblade‘s strongest element. There is constant feel of insanity and not only because of the voices in your head. The environment often changes, based on your mental state. When Senua just can’t bear it anymore, starts screaming in agony and despair, the voices in her head get louder and the world around you transforms into an even darker, dirty looking place. These are the most intense, atmospheric moments I have seen in a video game in a long time. And you often wonder if what you see is actually happening – you are in a very dark, mythical place after all – or if it all just takes place in your mind. Here reality becomes a very questionable concept.

While having incredible atmosphere, Hellblade’s combat system is pretty standard for the most part. You have light and heavy attacks, which you can use to perform combos, you can block, evade and parry (timing is important here), as well as a kick attack. The game does not tell you how to do any of these things, yet you will learn everything on your own in no time – which I find fascinating in a way. It is almost refreshing to have a game that does not flood the screen with button prompts and tutorial messages. You also have sort of a time-slowing power that charges over time. That one can be of great help in situations with multiple enemies. While the combat system might not be particularly innovative, it is very well implemented and definitely a lot of fun. In between the fights you mostly solve rune puzzles and those are probably the only thing I can truly criticise about the game. You usually have a closed gate with a rune on it, then you have to search for the image of this rune in the surrounding area. The image often consists of several objects in the environment, for instance, you have to look at a pole and part of a hut at the right angle. While I certainly enjoyed these puzzles, they were the weakest part of the game and they are the only reason Hellblade doesn’t get the highest possible score from me.

Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice is a story-driven experience that explores the gradual descent into psychosis of the protagonist – Senua. Its representation of mental illness can be eye-opening and disturbing at times, and the use of real-time motion capture and binaural audio design are impressive.

The puzzle-solving and pacing of the game can feel a little tedious at times, but these are inconsequential when considering the overall message or intention of the game. 

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is as beautiful as it is soul-crushing – a masterclass of atmosphere and conceptual design, and it is well worth the journey.

This game is visual and audio masterpiece. The acting is some of the best I've ever experienced from any protagonist in any game.

Warning: The focus of this game is the experience and NOT the gameplay. If you know that and still want to play, you will LOVE it. If you're looking for diverse combat and enemy variety, you will not. The difficulty slider will not make the game better.

That said, the enemies and environments you encounter are among the best desgined and fleshed out in any game ever.

Immersive, honest, and gorgeous. Totally recommend.

This is going to be one of those reviews that one would have a truckload to say about, yet when it comes to actually saying something, one ends up empty handed. I will try nonetheless. One thing is sure: playing [i]Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice[/i], was both a magnificent and harrowing experience. Ninja Theory, a development studio based on Cambridge, UK - one we may remember from [i]Enslaved: Odyssey to the West[/i] and the latest part of Devil May Cry series, [i]DmC: Devil May Cry[/i] - even though being relatively young in the market, accomplished an exceptional task with this game.

Here, we take on the role of Senua, a Pict warrior, hailing from Northern Scotland. All we know about her at the beginning of the game, is that Senua has lost her lover, Dillion, to a Viking raid and now she must take on a journey to the Nordic underworld: Helheim, to rescue him. The opening cinematic closely follows Senua as she journeys from the banks of Orkney to this supposed entrance to the underworld. A far away, soft and feminine voice starts talking about Senua's tragedy, and her unique, disturbing nature... and only when she hears the voice talking, and turns back towards the camera, directly looking at us, we realize Senua's sense of what is real may not be the reality that we all are aware of.

Okay, here, I'll start about that part which may be considered as spoilers, so be warned. [spoiler]Senua is a young Celtic warrior like no other: she is schizophrenic. This whole game, is much, much more than simply being a game. It is a direct medium designed to present the player the very experience of being schizophrenic. Our heroine will keep hearing voices, experience hallucinations, collect meaning from most trivial of natural occurrences and will go through periods of dire anxiety and paranoia. All that we encounter within the game, is how Senua interprets and experiences the reality, rather than an objective reality. Her journey to the underworld, her battles against the darkness, her combats with various gods, the challenges she continuously and ferociously overcome: are simply metaphors for her battle against the psychosis itself. At the end of the day, what actually happened to Senua is tragically simple: yet how she overcomes it, is a Herculean task nonetheless. [/spoiler]

What is downright marvelous about this game, is the character Senua herself. Melina Juergens, who performed Senua's voice acting and motion capturing throughout the game, presents an astonishing feat of acting. Her mimics, her tone, her gaze, her whole-body language continuously display a typhoon of emotions, practically enforcing you to live Senua's dark, horrific, painful reality. I strongly recommend watching the short documentary on the game after completing it, so you can witness the whole process yourself. Apparently, the developmental team worked with not only history professors for setting authenticity concerning Norse mythology and Celtic culture, yet they also worked with psychiatrists, specialists on psychosis and even psychotic patients themselves for an accurate representation. This whole creative process in no less than being fascinating!

I've already mentioned that the motion capture was used to enact characters. At this point, I also must note the Unreal Engine 4 presents a majestic scene when it comes to display a sense of realism. Textures, lights, colors and animations are no less than being breath-taking. This has been one VR worthy experience. I sadly lack the equipment, yet if you have a VR device, I strongly recommend trying. Another incredible display quality is the audio atmosphere of the game. [spoiler]As you keep playing, you'll keep hearing various voices, continuously commenting on your mood, your actions, your situation to better simulate paracusia, or auditory hallucinations.[/spoiler] Thus, playing the game with headphones on will hugely benefit to the atmosphere.

Let's talk gameplay at this point, shall we? The game may be categorized as an adventure game with action elements. You will travel through various parts of the said geography and handle endless visual and some auditory puzzles. Every now and then, you will face adversaries in the form of grotesque Viking warriors and even some of their gods. Puzzles are incredibly creative, yet some require an obsessive amount of attention to detail. I loved it since it adds to the atmosphere, yet I agree that it is not everyone’s cup of tea. You just should know what you'll be in for, when you are playing this game. It is a simulation and an experience, enwrapped within a historical setting and a story of tragedy. It is not your casual action-adventure; and it surely isn't the next [i]God of War[/i]. If you are looking for simply a bad-as s game, this is not it. If you are looking for a challenging experience which will test not only your skills, but your own psych: please try it. You won't be disappointed.

At the very beginning of the game, you will be warned that every time you fail, the rot on Senua's body will progress; and if you fail enough times, that would be the end of Senua's journey. [spoiler]This warning immediately started a rumor about a permadeath function about the game. According to the rumor, if you die enough times, your save games will be automatically erased, and you'll have to start over. Now, that is a brilliant hoax. The game says nothing about permadeath. You reach that conclusion based on a false impression yourself. There is no permadeath in the game. Yet, the warning and various following scenes are brilliantly places there to create that kind of assumption to feed into the horror factor. The game literally forces you to share Senua's reality, even though that might not be what is objectively real. I call that simply brilliant. [/spoiler]

At the end of the day, [i]Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice[/i] is a unique yet highly disturbing game, and one you won't soon forget. Please be warned, and try it, if you are willing to appreciate video games as a medium for art and a simulation on the more disturbing side.

Please also check out Lady Storyteller's Curator page [url=http://store.steampowered.com/curator/11672469/]here[/url] - follow for regular updates on reviews for other games!

Hmmm....this is a tough one to review. It is a game, but it's also a serious look at mental psychosis - and as such feels like it should be treated as a worthy endeavour, rather than rated outright as "entertainment". But on the other hand it is also entertainment, and an artistic / creative / technical undertaking, and so has to be viewed that way too.

Let me say first that I don't have any mental illness, nor do I know anyone who does - at least not to the extreme extent the main character suffers from. From that unenlightened position I would say it's a respectful and empathetic look at what it's like to live with that inner chaos, and it doesn't seem gratuitous with it's depiction of hallucinations and schizophrenia.

It takes you on a harrowing journey, that can be quite effectively disturbing in places. In truth it's more worthy as an educational tool about these conditions than it is as a game - at least in terms of gameplay mechanics. See - the problem with this project is that it is a game, and games are, well.....gamey. 

But they can't make it like God Of War because that's a step too far towards being disrespectful to the subject matter (and it was also an attempt to step away from AAA budgets, making it a smaller production), and if they didn't have at least some conventional gameplay it would just be a fairly thought provoking walking simulator.

So you have fighting, which symbolizes the heroines turmoil, but is also slightly stunted as far as combat goes. It's tactical, and has some seriously gorgeous special effects, yet isn't as freeflowing as most of it's ilk. The best comparison I can think of for the combat would be the Prince Of Persia (cel shaded) reboot from a while ago. 

You have puzzles, which tie in nicely to her unhinged perception of the world around her, but are pretty untaxing intellectually. Both systems have relevance to the theme, yet are only passable at best as far as mechanics go. They're more developed than just being padded fluff, but if you go into this game hoping for an epic best in class action title....you will be disappointed.    

Beyond these average features, and how it explores something unknowable unless you suffer from it yourself, there's the plot and the level of writing - both of which are nicely done. Artistically the game is immense, with some stunning visuals from a technical and design perspective. The audio is superb, with really evocative work done on the voices and sound effects - they advise you to play with headphones on, and it truly does enhance the experience. Senua is plagued by voices, and having them swirl around intimately within your own head is much more effective than just hearing them through speakers at a distance. 

So - two out of three for "value" so far, with a bit of a "meh" for the actual gameplay. The length of the game is fairly short - I think I took 6 hours or so to finish it, so that should be considered too. It's complete, runs well, is glitch free, and is quite responsive to control. It's not a product that will disappoint in those regards, but if you can't immerse yourself in the otherworldly sights and sounds (this is crass - but they are quite trippy), or get drawn in by the plot, then there isn't much for you here. 

As an interactive experience this is incredible, and has a level of craftmanship that is quite rare, but as a game it's only so so.

If you liked this review, and want to see more, then why not check out my curator page here:
https://steamcommunity.com/groups/The_dull_games_reviewer

A really enjoyable experience. The game itself is just a vessel to convey a story, a tragic, and one that offers one of the most effective portrayals of psychosis in media. For this alone it is incredible. The voice cast and binaural audio is something that absolutely has to be experienced and it's pretty relentless. The experience is at times haunting, terrifying, and disturbing.

Playing this in one playthrough, although achievable is very difficult because I feel it can take a toll on you. I highly recommend headphones for full immersion.

The story itself is dark, at times overwhelmingly so, but there are some profound messages and the story is interesting enough. The deeper meanings underlying the story can at times be confusing and it's definitely something you'll be thinking about more after the game ends. It's not a perfect story, but it's very good.

The gameplay mechanics aren't really what this is about; at times it might feel somewhat tiring to solve puzzles. Sometimes the speed of the character is frustrating, as smooth as the animations are. But there are mechanics which are obviously designed to be frustrating as this brings about additional fatigue upon the player, which I believe is fully intended.

Although the combat system is not particularly deep, it has enough depth to be enjoyable, and the variety of foes that you face given the intended length of the game is roughly what you'd expect. There's some great innovation displayed by the game and there are some really memorable moments, amongst some that are less so.

I highly recommend this game and I believe that Ninja Theory have taken a risk that has paid off. In my view this is one of the most important games to surface in a long time. Without a question it is a perfect example of what makes video games art.  This is legitimate art.

If you have any experience with psychosis, I wouldn't recommend that you play the game, it would be very difficult to do so. If you have experienced other mental health problems, it might be a bit upsetting at times, but it's manageable.

Probably the most immersive game I've ever played and definitely one of the most beautiful. The audio is also on another level compared to any other game on the market. So on of the first things you'll see when starting the game is a disclaimer about how they worked with psychologist to create a realistic depiction of psychosis and that people who suffer from psychosis may find it disturbing. Don't assume that's just a "We hope nobody is offended" type of statement, like I did. I have psychosis, and just the opening scene, the voices in her head (especially since I had surround sound headphones on) triggered my own psychosis. I had to take a break about 1-2 minutes in, but decided that I was so impressed with the depiction of it that I would calm myself down and keep playing. Her hallucinations are done so well, the live action rotoscoped people she hallucinates are so uncanny and uncomfortable (My own hallucinations don't look anything like that so I can't say how accurate that part is). Now typing it out it sounds like a very backhanded compliment, but I actually really appreciate how much effort was put into depicting her psychosis in a way that was so real to me that it instantly triggered my own. [h2] The story tells about... [/h2]
...the Pictish warrior Senua, who suffers from severe psychosis. She embarks on a journey into the depths of Helheim to save the soul of her beloved Dillion. The plot of the game is tied to Senua's disease much deeper than it might seem at the beginning. The game also tells a lot of Scandinavian legends (people who played God of War 4 will notice the similarities). The game itself is small. There are no side quests, and the main plot takes place in an average of 8 hours. There are a total of 14 achievements in the game, 13 of which are story-driven.

[h2] Gameplay [/h2]
The main part of the gameplay consists of battles and solving puzzles. There are about four types of puzzles that can get boring in the middle of the game (this is what many consider to be a boring part of the gameplay and quit the game because of this). The game has a good combat system. Senua fights with a sword, and can also focus (enemies become more vulnerable, slow). The enemies are presented in the form of about five types of monsters and three bosses. All this is more than enough to ensure that the action game does not get bored during the entire passage.

[h2] Environment and design [/h2]
The game was created on the UE4 engine — the graphics are pleasant, but the optimization is average (friezes were often observed). Although there is no open world in the game (it is not needed here), all locations are diverse and well-designed.

[h2] Total [/h2]
This video game is interesting because the developers were able to show a wide audience the state of psychosis. It has a good plot and action, good graphics and musical accompaniment. However, some people may get bored with the gameplay with its abundance of monotonous puzzles. It is important to note that throughout the passage you will be whispered by the inner voices of Senua (they, by the way, will help you during the fight). This is important to consider, as it may annoy some players.

[b] I recommend purchasing the game at a 90% discount (especially now, before the release of the second part), and before buying, take into account the nuances that I described above. [/b]

[h2] Сюжет игры [/h2]
История рассказывает про пиктскую воительницу Сенуа, страдающую тяжелым психозом. Она отправляется в путешествие в глубины Хельхейма, чтобы спасти душу своего возлюбленного Диллиона. Сюжет игры завязан на болезни Сенуа намного глубже, чем может показаться в начале. В игре также рассказывается много скандинавских легенд (люди, игравшие в God of War 4, заметят схожести). Игра сама по себе небольшая. В ней нет дополнительных квестов, а основной сюжет проходится в среднем за 8 часов. Всего в игре 14 достижений, 13 из которых — сюжетные. 

[h2] Геймплей [/h2]
Основная часть геймплея состоит из сражений и разгадывания головоломок. Так называемых головоломок присутствует примерно четыре типа, которые могут надоесть уже в середине игры (именно это многие считают скучной частью геймплея и бросают из-за этого игру). В игре неплохая боевая система. Сенуа сражается мечом, а также может сосредотачиваться (враги становятся более уязвимыми, медлительными). Враги представлены в виде примерно пяти типов монстров и трех боссов. Всего этого более чем достаточно для того, чтобы боёвка не надоела за всё время прохождения.

[h2] Окружение и дизайн [/h2]
Игра создана на движке UE4 — графика приятная, но оптимизация средняя (часто наблюдались фризы). Хотя в игре нет открытого мира (он тут и не нужен), все локации разнообразны и хорошо проработаны. 

[h2] Итог [/h2]
Эта видеоигра интересна тем, что разработчики смогли показать широкой аудитории состояние психоза. В ней неплохой сюжет и боёвка, хорошая графика и музыкальное сопровождение. Правда, некоторым геймплей может надоесть своим обилием однообразных головоломок. Важно отметить, что на протяжении всего прохождения вам будут шептать внутренние голоса Сенуа (они, кстати, будут вам помогать во время драки). Это важно учитывать, так как некоторых игроков это может раздражать. 

[u] Рекомендую приобретать игру по скидке 90% (особенно сейчас, перед выходом второй части), а перед покупкой учитывать нюансы, которые я описал выше. [/u]

One of the most outstanding and captivating video game experiences I have ever had the pleasure of playing. Their depiction of Schizophrenia is  about as accurate as you can get in a video game, from the pattern recognition to the visual and audio hallucinations. I really like that there isn't anything on the screen besides Senua-- no minimap, no waypoints, no health bar, just voices in your head. This makes it incredibly immersive. Using good headphones is an absolute must to get the full effect of the binaural audio. This game is so incredible, one of the best games I've ever played , a masterpiece!

The game opens with a warning that it was made with people who have experienced psychosis and asks you to take it seriously. It means this. Take it seriously. Ninja Theory consulted extensively with neuroscientists and people who live with psychosis to get this right, and they got it right. With headphones on, the voices move around your head in three dimensional space. They notice things before you do. They disagree about what is happening. Sometimes they try to help. The effect is not gimmicky. It is genuinely immersive and occasionally genuinely distressing in a way that feels completely intentional and respectful.

Lines from the Creator of this masterpiece...

"Mental illness has been with us as long as we have been on this earth, but why ? Why hasn't evolution stamped out this weakness from within our gene pool ? I often Pondered this question until I realized that the question had an in-built flaw. It assumes that being and thinking differently is a weakness. The only reason we have computers, spacecraft, medicine, poetry, art and yes even video-games, is because individuals were able to simulate new abstract realities in their mind and share them with the rest of us. We need people to be willing to see differently in order for us to progress as a society. And we need to be open to these new ways of seeing. I so dislike Steam's thumbs up / thumbs down system. While it works for big numbers, it means the single review is forced to lose a lot of nuance. And while this is not an issue for games you know for certain you liked or disliked, when it comes to Hellblade, I'm struggling a bit more. But let's start from the beginning.

"You really should play this game. The gameplay's not very great, but the story is soo good."

More or less, these were the words a few of my friends used to convince me I should give Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice a chance. I have to say I didn't trust their judgement too much, but I decided, what the hell, maybe they're right, maybe this is actually a very good game.

"Game." That's exactly the point with Senua's Sacrifice, isn't it? If there's one thing I realized one hour into the game and was only reinforced as I went on, was that Ninja Theory's effort is not a good "game". It has a very nice story, sure, although narrated in a way that I felt was a bit too long winded for my liking, and with an ending that I can't really say left me satisfied. But overall, it's a good story, with some very intense moments. The narrative department definitely deserves any credit they received for the work they did. 

But the gameplay? Oh man. Let's be clear here: Ninja Theory is not an unexperienced studio when it comes to action games. They've got at least three relatively big action-oriented titles under their belt (Heavenly Sword, Enslaved, and Devil May Cry). I think it's entirely reasonable to expect that they should have it figured out, but clearly that's not the case. While certainly flashy, the combat in Hellblade, from a mechanical standpoint, is absolutely uninteresting, relying on a simple rock paper scissors system paired with terribly sluggish movement. As is often the case in action games, not getting flanked is of paramount importance in Hellblade as well, but proper positioning is made artificially more annoying by the fact that your only option for finding it is dodge spam, since Senua will otherwise either walk around very slowly or charge straight at the enemy. The combat itself is also not particularly challenging, even on hard, but I don't think that's necessarily a drawback in a narrative-focused game.

"But you just said it yourself! Combat is not the main part of the game. That's Senua's story", I know some will argue. And I agree; the meat of Hellblade, what distinguishes it from other games, is the story portrayed, its themes and the clever and well-executed use of the voices. But if the gameplay is a secondary part, it's still a significant secondary part. There's a lot of fighting in Senua's Sacrifice, a lot of time spent flailing your sword around and parrying and dodging. With none of it being particularly entertaining, and while it might not be the main focus of the game, it's still there and it ends up detracting from the overall experience. 

Another thing that there's a lot of in Senua is puzzles. I'm not even sure "puzzles" is the right word, seeing as pretty much all of them require absolutely zero brain power except for the little amount required to walk where you need to be in order to line up what needs to be lined up. And look, I get it - the puzzles are supposed to be an allegory for the fact that Senua sees things other people don't and the runes carry power with them and all that stuff. But that's just the reason they're there; that's not an excuse for how absolutely boring they are and how much of a waste of time they feel.

So puzzles are another one of Hellblade's weak points. What else is there to talk about? Ah, right: the minor stuff that separates a good game from one that leaves a mark. Stuff like the audio department, for example. Even here, Hellblade seems to have a split soul: the voices are definitely a positive, at the very least when they're used to convey plot points. I found them honestly annoying during combat and during general exploration (for example during puzzle solving), but there's a point to be made that when you have voices in your head you can't just shut them off when you want to, and I think that's a fair point. But even here Hellblade doesn't seem to be able to get everything right, does it? While the amount of effort put into the voices in Senua's head is nothing short of stunning, beside that the audio direction is not particularly remarkable. There are only two audio tracks that had me think "Hey, that's not too bad", and they are both at the very end. The rest of the game seems to have just a few not particularly inspired ambient tracks and a battle track that's like, decent I guess?

Another small thing I found mostly unremarkable is the general world design. It's not bad per se, it's just what you would expect your average viking fantasy landscape to look like, except with a lot more dead people and ruined houses. The enemies and with them the bosses also suffer from this. Valraven is fast dude with a thing for feather crows, Surt isn't even a giant, it's just an impressively tall man (but not significantly more so that other regular enemies you will meet), Garm is a big dog, and Hela is just... well, you know where I'm going with this.

So the story's good. Really good, in fact. But Senua's story cannot carry the rest of the game on its own. Hellblade suffers from too many drawbacks, too many things, minor and not, that it doesn't get quite right or that it botches completely. And while I could be inclined to forgive that in a studio that lacks experience or funding, that's definitely not the case for Ninja Theory. 

So to conclude: if you're interested in the game, my personal recommendation is that you should watch a playthrough of it on Youtube, to spare yourself the ugliness and get the good parts. And if you want to know what a game where the gameplay supports the story rather than actively hampering it looks like, I suggest you play either Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons or Celeste.

I've always liked linear games, not only because the devs focus more on the story that anything else but also you don't have any filler. It's always nice to play a linear game after the tons and tons of open world's, and this one delivers the story as an experience, you will accompany and help Senua on her quest, will hear the northmen's stories along the way and challenge yourself to solve the not so complicated puzzles.

Highly recommended, I believe anyone could get into this game and manage to battle their way through Hellheim without trouble. I don't know much about psychology but I think the way Senua's psychosis was represented here was really good, use headphones please, there's no other way to get the best of Hellblade.

What an absolutely terrific game from start to finish!

I think you can say that Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is, in it's core, a third-person action-adventure, mixing together some environmental puzzles, bit's of wandering around the scenery and close-combat sword fighting.

You play the epynomous heroine Senua, traveling through a mythical land, trying to reach Hel to bring back her deceased love Dillion.

The game creates a very strong, eery, chilling atmosphere through it's sound and voiceover and graphics, which are beautiful.
Especially the motion capture stands out as does the voice acting. It's brilliantly done and i can't recommend enough to play the game with headphones, it's just so much better.

The game doesn't really take your hand, but it shouldn't take long to figure everything out, it's not that complex.

The whole presentation of the story, the journey of Senua and the whole depiction her mental illness is very well done.
From the beginning, you'll hear voices that guide you, help out, warn you and give you little tipps, besides giving you some backstory and exposition. There's no HUD to help you out otherwise, no health indicator on you or your enemies (you only get visual clues on how badly they are injured) and no markers whatsoever (which are not necessarily needed, as it's quite linear with some bigger hubs and labyrinth-like levels).

The combat is very intense, personal and feels very raw and brutal. 
You don't have that much enemy types, but each has it's own way of fighting and it's own tactic to defeat it.
Puzzles are challenging, but i've never felt that they were too hard, you really have to listen to the voices and check your environment to figure everything out but it's very rewarding once you did that.

I did struggle twice witth some camera issues in combat, which then resulted in death and for one or the other puzzle i felt that i ran a bit too much around to figure it out.
You could also argue that the combat is somewhat repetitive, though i never felt that it was tedious. Apart from those small things, i think it's an awesome game and would recommend it to everyone that likes action-adventures with sword-combat. puzzles and a bit of a walking simulator in between.

[h1]Is Hellblade really a masterpiece?[/h1]

From the opening scenes, [b]Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice (HSS)[/b] certainly sucks you into the eerily dark, meaty, mind-warping world of Helheim. Travelling to the Viking Hell to save the soul of your beloved, your eyes play tricks on you and the ever pessimistic, incessant voices in your head do their best to mock every decision you make. The psychosis is intense at times. With every painful step Senua takes forward in her quest, her sense of reality & her sanity are challenged.

Throughout Senua's quest you learn more about Senua’s past & reasons to why she would journey through hell to save her loved one. This main story arc plus the rune lore stones which pepper the game levels provide a consistent stream of grim stories of the Norse Gods & other tragic tales of man. These chilling tales are all beautifully acted and voiced with great emotional impact. The quality of the acting really sets [b]HSS[/b]  a notch above most & coupled with the immersive directional soundscape including multiple voices in your head & creepy environmental effects the audio is some of the best I have ever heard in a game! Turn it up!
http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1161977457 The claustrophobic camera views, although can be frustrating at times, offer some great close up action & showcase Senua's detailed character model. [b]HSS[/b]  blends illusionary effects & cut-scene transitions smoothly not relinquishing your control for too long. It adds further complexity to combat too by challenging you to keep enemies off your six since you cannot easily see behind you.

Combat started out being fun for me but got boring & repetitive rather quickly. Your foe are big & intimidating, action looks brutal, but there is a lot of rolling and attacks, odd block then rolling some more. As you progress, the number of enemies increase making for some long dull fights or frustrating enough to have you quitting. You replay the same mobs throughout the game. Boss fights were more creative & enjoyable, but did tend to be a bit long winded too. No HUD or health bars also can make it difficult to see your progress against enemies but generally [b]HSS[/b]  is fairly forgiving not to really need it.

The level design was one area that was not as good as I hoped. The symbol door puzzles & illusions I enjoyed solving. These were fresh & although not overly complex it broke up the linear design to a degree. The issue I had with it was that the same formula was reused heavily for a large number of level sections. It became predictable. All levels are visually rich & unique looking for the most, but seem intentionally limited, with any open area solely reserved for fight sequences for example & almost always there being a puzzle door to unlock.
http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1291036470 For such a highly detailed game, some of the low quality textures do stand out in some scenes/angles too. Other graphical details like the eyes watching you from inside a rock or tree, vision flashes/scene changes & masterful use of lighting[i](darkness?)[/i] do a great job to counter any shortcomings. With most graphical details enabled I could maintain around 60fps on my 1080ti, but did see semi-frequent frame drops down to 45-55fps during cut-scene transitions & other random areas. Not greatly impacting gameplay due to its pace, but was visible occasionally.

[b]HSS[/b] hits it out the park when it comes to its gritty, emotion filled, Viking tragedy. An engaging character & story, captivating performances, graphically impressive with an exceptional auditory experience it will immerse you into Senua’s nightmare from beginning to end. Although I would fall just shy of calling it a masterpiece as I wasn't a fan of the repetitious combat & some levels left me feeling like a [i]rat-in-a-maze[/i], I still thoroughly enjoyed the journey into madness. 

Overall, hellishly recommended; would sacrifice myself again!

[h1]Haunting & Beautiful // Recommended for Those Seeking an Experience in Intensity[/h1]

+ Absolutely breathtaking visuals
+ Outstanding voice-acting & facial animations
+ Combat is simple & straightforward without a lot of gimmicks; the game gives you the tools you need from the beginning of the game & really doesn't change them, but works around what you've been given to increase the challenge as you progress
+ Two of the three boss battles (not including Hela) are excellent & challenging; Surtr was perhaps a little too easy & Fenrir was extremely challenging but fair (fans of Monster Hunter or Dark Souls would probably feel right at home with that one)
+ Devs kept mechanics simple & were careful to give you an enriching experience without too much baggage; the complete absence of things like inventory, usable items, & non-narrative character progression would seriously hurt most other games of the genre, but really holds the game up in this case
+ Intensely atmospheric, often unsettling, & not without a bevy of very effective emotional moments
+ Is very creative & participative in the way it handles such a complex & delicate subject as mental illness; I'm a health care professional & I can say this was spot on in my experiences (I felt more affected by this game with a good pair of headphones than I did running simulations in school for things like voice-hearing, for example)
+ Game was admittedly short, but well-paced & I felt I got my money's-worth
+ Blessedly short load-times, although some of this may come down to the hardware you're using
+ The "collectible" lore stones were engrossing to say the least; I really appreciated a gifted voice-actor/storyteller filling the player in on Norse mythology & I was eager to find them
+ Puzzles were creative & fairly straightforward without being too easy
+ Some of the challenges & environments in the game (most notably the Shard Trials) were extremely inventive in their presentation

- Even though this game has gone through a few patches & hot-fixes from its release, I still had about two or three instances of puzzles being bugged, forcing a restart of the section I was in
- The ending left me slightly dissatisfied, although it wasn't terrible: Senua's story was technically resolved, although the implications were a little vague & I desperately wanted to know what became of her after (felt like sequel-bait in some ways, though I have trouble picturing what an actual sequel would look like, if that makes sense)

HELLBLADE: SENUA'S SACRIFICE, is a game about Psychosis and mental illnes. Here is what I can telll you:

Where do I start. Well.... My sister has been having multiple psychotic episodes in the last 7 years. Some even lasting years. She would tell me she could hear voices and see things. I never really understood what she meant. While eating dinner together at the dinner table, she would look around as if she was looking for something or listening to someone. This went on for years. Psychiatrists told my family and I that the reason she was psychotic was due to severe trauma from classmates bullying her. She admitted this later to us. The problem with psychosis is, that the imaginary worlds (like the one my sister creates for herself) end up looking real and very realistic. I was shocked to find that this game portaits psychosis so well. I'm afraid of letting my sister hear/play this game. I hope, once (if) she gets better, she can play this game and understand herself what she was experiencing.

This game is a must play. it helped me understand my sister's point of view better. My sister sleeps about 18 hours of the day because of her  dangerous and heavy medication and because being psychotic is very mentally draining. I noticed this myself when playing Senua. I couldn't play more than about 1.5 hours before needing a long break. It was just so immersive.

The Story and Graphics are amazing. The voices Senua hears are mind twisting,and horrifying.
The combat is not that amazing in my opinion. Very simplistic and sometimes repetitive.
The underlaying story is amazing and I won't say a thing because I want to let you experience this for yourself.
Everybody's story is different. The hardest battles are fought in the mind. If anything, that's what my sister and Senua have made absolutely clear to me.

[h1]Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice[/h1]
[b]Disturbing and original plot[/b]
Hellblade gives us a premise that shocks us from the first moment and already shows that the game doesn't think small at all. [i]Senua[/i] is a warrior of the Celtic people exiled for a time from her tribe who returns and finds her then husband [i]Dillion[/i] dead due to a Viking invasion that took place there. Furious, the warrior vows to rescue her beloved from the depths of Hellheim, the Viking hell. And this is where our journey begins, with Senua arriving in Viking territory ready to face all risks to rescue her husband.

[b]The premise seems interesting, but seen from this angle it is not surprising. However, an aspect that is far from being a mere detail of this plot is that [i]Senua[/i] suffers from a serious mental illness called Schizophrenia. For those who don't know, this is a disease marked by unusual behaviors and confusion between what is real and what isn't. The main symptoms of schizophrenia (also known as psychosis in some ways) are delusions, auditory and visual hallucinations, distorted thoughts, and poor social interaction.[/b]

Due to several aspects of her life, in addition to the trauma of seeing the person she loved most in life brutally dead, [i]Senua[/i] goes into a crisis and begins to have delusions involving her life story, her traumas and all your anxieties. Throughout the game, you constantly wonder what is real and what is part of the protagonist's delusion. And what initially seems like a “[b]God of War[/b]” turns out to be much more, which is fantastic.

The game's narrative is engaging, deep and fragmented. But everything has an explanation and is designed to cause the player the impressions necessary for him to become emotionally involved with the protagonist of the story. A plot immersion like that can only be compared to [b]The Last of Us[/b] which is incredible for an independent production made by just over ten people.

[h1]The hallucinations turned into a game[/h1]
Talking directly to the game's story, we have its visuals that need no comment. It is one of the most beautiful graphics. Senua's facial expressions and performances, the result of motion capture technology, only increase the character's expressiveness and depth. In addition, the world around you, all set in Nordic culture, is beautiful and, at the same time, scary. Beautiful landscapes and horrendous locations contrast all the time creating a phenomenal look.

But it's not just beautiful graphics that [b]Hellblade[/b] is all about. The entire game world speaks to the protagonist's story on different levels, making everything from the cameras to the enemies we face into a single story told by all the senses at the same time. It's amazing to see how the developers managed to play around with auditory and visual perception in the game so that the player really sees himself inside the skin of a person with schizophrenia.

The game is focused on solving puzzles mixed with moments of action. As for the puzzles, everything around you can be part of the experience. The notion of perspective built into each map, allowing one to explore its nuances and thus find the right angles, gives access to paths that were once simply not there. The game messes with the map around you at all times, causing the player to get confused thinking “was that already there before?” at various points in the game.

[h1]Challenging combats, but mere details[/h1]
The other part of the game is fighting enemies that simply appear in the middle of nowhere to threaten Senua's journey (you decide if they are illusion or not). Viking enemies are rotten and monstrous, reminiscent of something between the [b]Dark Souls[/b] franchise and the aforementioned [b]God of War[/b]. The combat itself is also somewhat reminiscent of these two games, but with a level of difficulty not as absurd as that of the Souls series. But that doesn't stop him from being very challenging.

[b]Hellblade[/b], right at its beginning, presents a clear message that you have a fixed number of kills you can have before you lose all your story advancement and simply start from scratch. This keeps the player alert to dangers and prevents them from simply killing themselves to start over with full stamina. But this is one of the only written warnings you will have on your screen.

To make both the gameplay as a whole, as well as the combats themselves much more tense and immersive, Hellblade has absolutely no data written on screen. Health or energy bar, enemy health or damage number. Nothing just appears on the screen that isn't really part of Senua's perception. This makes the game more immersive and challenging, especially in combat.

Even the most common enemies need more than ten hits to kill. Also, the game's challenge curve starts to rise a lot after we get to the halfway point. And this is all faced "with the naked eye", without any kind of material given to make it easier to know if the enemy is almost dying, if you're on the right path, if your health is low or anything like that.

But make no mistake, the game is still didactic in the right measure for not having this kind of thing. It is designed in a way that its map, its landscapes, the behavior of the enemies and its vision pass all this information in a very organic way. You don't need to know how much health the enemy has, just see how many cuts your sword has already made in their skin and notice how their speed is decreasing, as well as their attacks.

[h1]Never played anything like it[/h1]

First of all, anyone trying this game should come in with an open mind to experience a narrative that builds slowly, focusing far less on an action-oriented gameplay and much more on something deeply personal to the protagonist, Senua - a Scottish warrior afflicted with, or perhaps gifted with, the ability to hear voices. The emphasis is on her story, her emotions and the mystery of what awaits her at the end. The pacing is slow and you’ll pick up a good amount of Norse lore as you traverse the land of the Northmen. Having played God of War (2018), I felt right at home with the mythological elements, though playing GoW is by no means a pre-requisite. Some players might feel disinterested early on, as the game can feel like a walking simulator at times. To them, I’d say: stick with it for at least the first three hours i.e., up to the completion of the initial two main quests. The game truly picks up after that and becomes spectacular. Some of the later areas especially the Blindness trial, are absolutely phenomenal leaving me speechless. I was blown away that such a personal, impactful experience could even be created. With “darkness” being a central theme, there were moments that really tested my nerves, yet I found myself even more eager to see what came next. In a way, the game helped me confront my own fears, just as the protagonist is meant to. Although I have a 5.1 speaker setup, I found that playing with headphones (as the game itself recommends), made for a far richer experience, especially with the constant voices whispering in your ears.         Controlling the character is simple and basic even in combat. You start with no tutorial but the game is played in a way that you will not need one sine she can hear voices that will give you tips throughout the game.

        There are some mobs and bosses that will appear throughout the game, but the combats are more like a filler part and a way to change the pace of the game.         You need to solve puzzles to progress, they are not hard to solve, it is more of a search and find kind of puzzle. The voices in her head and the glowing runes will help you, which makes it a lot easier.

        There are Lore stones, which contains of some cool stories and it unlocks an achievement.

"They say dreams are visions of our memories, thoughts and fears as seen by our inner eye. What if each one of us is always dreaming, even when awake? Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is a narrative-focused, cinematic game that could be described as part walking simulator and part psychological horror. It follows the story of a Celtic warrior named Senua who journeys to Hel (Viking underground) with the aim of rescuing the soul of her dead lover. 

Senua suffers from psychosis, and the game is both a depiction of her journey to Hel and the exploration of the roots of her trauma. Symbolically, Senua journeys both forward as she comes closer to Hel and backwards in time as she experiences flashbacks that reveal her past. Thus the story of Senua's journey unfolds on two levels which intertwine throughout the game. 

Senua is not alone on her journey: she is accompanied by an omniscient narrator, an unidentified female voice that possesses intimate knowledge of Senua's feelings, thoughts and motivations, and ocassionally advised by the spirit of a shaman who pledged to guide Senua in this life and the next. She also hears a number of different other unnamed voices – hallucinations brought on by the psychosis. They follow Senua from the very start of the game, alternately mocking, helping, scaring, guiding, belittling and encouraging her. They will help Senua by telling her what to do in combat or when she's solving puzzles, they will simultaneously cheer her on and doubt her capability to continue, they will root for her but also mock her when she struggles. I am not sure whether they reflect Senua's fears, insecurities and self-doubt, or whether they are meant to represent society's mistreatment of the mentally ill; possibly they are a combination of both. 

Two key characteristics of psychosis are visual/aural hallucinations and delusions. A person suffering from a psychotic mental illness perceives the world in a fundamentally different way, and this is what Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice attempts to portray as faithfully as possible. The visual and sound design is fully employed in the service of this purpose, frequently distorting the world around Senua and assaulting her with a cacophony of sounds at times. The sound design is masterfully crafted, making the player feel like the voices that Senua hallucinates are coming from every direction, adding to the oppressive, anxiety-inducing atmosphere of the game. The puzzles are also all built around the notion that Senua sees the world differently, by seeing meaningful patterns in random world geometry and perceiving things that were initially not there by looking at the world from a different perspective. 

One drawback of the game is that large chunks of it can be characterized as a walking simulator as the gameplay is not very interactive. These parts are interrupted by sequences with combat or puzzle solving. The puzzles are not very difficult, occasionally they may even be rather simplistic, but thematically they fit the narrative perfectly. The combat is solid, although a bit shallow as Senua has only a limited range of actions she can do with her sword (the usual light and heavy attacks, a running attack, block and evade). The emphasis on combat is not very big, but the few boss battles there are in the game are very well done. There is a particular feeling of suspense present during combat due to the fact that there is no HUD in the game and thus no indication of how many hits Senua can take, or how many she needs to deliver to her enemies to bring them down. 

This lack of gameplay information is present in the rest of the game as well: a prompt to interact with a door, for example, will not show up if Senua approaches it – instead the player has to figure out on their own that they need to hit a specific button if they want to climb, open a door or drop down a ledge. Obviously by removing the HUD the developers strived to instil a deeper sense of immersion, but this can lead to some frustration occasionally when the player approaches a door and hits the interact button only for it to have no effect, leaving the player to wonder if there's a bug with the door or if they failed to solve some other puzzle to make the door open. But no, it's not a puzzle problem – there seems to be some kind of bug with a couple of doors in the game and the player needs to move back and forth a bit to find the exact spot where they need to stand for the interact button to work. 

Overall the game is a very unique experience, although how much you will enjoy it depends on how much you can empathize with people suffering from mental illness. The developers went out of their way to consult researchers and people with mental illnesses in an effort to portray psychosis as honestly as possible. An emphatic person will experience strong, at moments visceral, reaction to certain things portrayed in this game, certain combat sequences and/or scenes of Senua's mental anguish. I felt chills running down my spine at some of these moments; at others, I felt intense sadness and sympathy for Senua. Others might find large parts of the game boring because big chunks of it are not very interactive. The game is also very linear and there is not much exploring or collecting to be done. I didn't find that to be a drawback in this kind of game which is obviously much more focused on experiencing the narrative. The only real problem I had was that the subtitles were often not completely in sync with the narration.

This game is unique. It deals with serious, difficult and unfortunately all too often ignored topics about mental illnesses such as depression and schizophrenia. In doing so, hallucinations, traumas, fears, psychoses and delusions are portrayed well and realistically, for which the developers have also brought many experts on board. For this reason alone, you should definitely play it.

[b]Psychosis[/b]

This is an important theme when it comes to Hellblade's story. Senua, while on the journey to find his dead lover's soul frequently has visions (hallucinations), sees or hears things that are not really there and even struggles with herself. Often cutscenes include Senua speaking incoherently while she is convinced that she is fighting an entity known as Darkness.

[b]Norse mythology[/b]

It's nice to have characteristics from the Norse mythology included along with Celtic elements. We venture into Helheim to fight with Hela. Again, this is all nice but please bear in mind the above paragraph with our heroine's mental illness. It can easily stop you from enjoying this game - Hellblade is very unique in this sense but not everybody will appreciate Senua's constant struggle with her mind between duels.

[b]Graphics + game mechanics[/b]

The game looks tremendously beautiful. Melina Juergens's motion capture is great and the voice acting (which is an important part of the story) is also superb. To a certain degree Hellblade can be considered a work of art. Too bad it is relatively short and the overall presentation is marred by the lacklustre game mechanics.

What is the issue here? Well, we can attack (low and high attacks), block and roll over. The problem is that sections sometimes only pose an extra challenge by sending against us more enemies. And to make this very annoying the newly-spawned creatures attack from behind. You'll often feel that some of these sequences drag on and on and you just wish they were over.

Additionally, puzzle solving sequences will be frequent. Our task will be to look for certain symbols. Using the environment for this purposes i.e. aligning various  - for instance, hanging - objects to get the desired shape looks fun at the beginning but gets boring very soon. 

[b]Summary[/b]

Hellblade is a very interesting game. I do not recall playing anything else with this much focus on disorders. This stops the constant action so some players will feel like being cheated. There is a menu with a documentary - consider it a "making-of" video - that provides more explanation on the background as well as on the developing process. It is certainly very interesting and Senua's Sacrifice is a must play if you don't mind playing something unique that requires a bit more time to process.

Let me make one thing very clear about this game: it's not for everyone. 

The story, graphics, and characterizations are all absolutely top notch. Senua is a truly sympathetic, tragic character, and the story deals with complex themes of psychosis/phobias, abuse, trauma, and dogmatism. It's also one of the greatest representations of mental illness (beyond anxiety and depression) I've seen in any piece of media. For all that, I do recommend the game on principle. 

That said, what might turn a lot of people away from the game is the actual gameplay. It's basically an interactive story/walking simulator, with puzzles and hack and slash action sprinkled in. 

Senua moves very slowly (even when running), and the puzzles range from fairly straightforward to needing a guide in order to progress. When I first started playing I almost dropped it completely because one puzzle was very difficult; I had to force myself to power through so I could get to the good stuff later. 

There are also a lot of scenes that are very dependant on your sense of hearing and vision (and the subtitles are pretty poor quality and don't match what's being said all the time), so if you're Deaf/hard of hearing or visually impaired, forget it.  

This is a game that will take some patience but when it gets good, it gets REALLY good and will make the experience absolutely worth it. Hopefully the sequel will improve on the gameplay and accessibility because I'm genuinely stoked for more.
